title: On‑Prem BGP Route‑Flap — Runbook Sketch & Incident Notes
content:
Summary:

Short summary: During a customer on‑prem maintenance window a subset of control‑plane prefixes were intermittently withdrawn by the customer edge, causing control‑plane reachability loss for a handful of Private deployments. The visible symptoms included API timeouts from customer apps, failed health checks to control endpoints, and flapping x509 validation errors in the vendor agent. Impact window ~2025‑11‑05 03:12–03:47 UTC for most affected tenants; some recovered earlier via route convergence.

Primary impact areas:
- Redwood Private control plane (customer‑facing endpoints) unreachable from customer VPC/subnets for 10–35 minutes per tenant.
- Automated deployment/health‑check jobs failed (k8s probes timed out).
- Customer oncall saw elevated error rates, retries increased, partial failover to hosted API for a few integrations.

How we detected it:
- Pager alert: control_plane_endpoint_5xx_rate >= 5% for > 5m (from Redwood Console -> Route: private‑eu).
- SRE oncall observed correlated traceroutes showing next‑hop blackholing.
- BGP telemetry from partner router (where available) showed prefix withdrawals at 03:12 UTC and repeated reannouncements.
- tcpdump on customer edge showed TCP RSTs for the control plane port during the flap windows.

Timeline (high level):
- 03:09 UTC: maintenance announced by customer NOC (later confirmed).
- 03:12 UTC: first withdrawal of /32 control‑plane prefix from customer AS (observed in BGP stream).
- 03:15 UTC: Redwood Console alerts and rate increase; first oncall page.
- 03:17–03:25 UTC: intermittent reachability — some tenants showed full recovery after BGP reconverge, others continued flapping.
- 03:27 UTC: SRE escalated to networking lead; confirmed with customer NOC that a route‑map change was pushed as part of maintenance.
- 03:35–03:47 UTC: customer rolled back the route‑map change; stable routes restored; all health checks recovered.

Root cause analysis (working hypothesis):
- Immediate trigger: customer applied a route‑map in maintenance that unintentionally matched a control‑plane /32 aggregation and set next‑hop to NULL (or prepended community that caused local policy to blackhole).
- Contributing factors:
  - Control plane prefixes are relatively specific (/32 /128) and not pinned by persistent BGP attributes (localpref/communities) that force preferencing during maintenance.
  - No automated validation between customer change and expected critical prefix advertisements (we lacked an automated guardrail that would flag removal of expected control plane prefixes).
  - Some customer firewall policies were stateful with aggressive TCP inspection; temporary asymmetric routing during the flap caused connection resets.

Why this caused high user impact:
- Control endpoints are single‑prefix reachable from customer edge; withdrawal equals outright loss rather than degraded latency.
- Several automation systems assume short control plane outages are safe — but our cert handshake and long‑running connections timed out and required reconnects, causing cascading retries.

Mitigations performed during incident:
- Tier 2 SRE contacted customer NOC and asked them to check the recent route‑map and undo changes (they confirmed rollback at 03:36 UTC).
- As an interim engineering mitigation we temporarily altered our BGP export policy on the peering fabric to advertise an aggregate that preserved reachability for the control plane (limited, rapid step — only used when customer rollback delayed).
- Increased alerting sensitivity for control plane prefix withdrawals and automatic paging for SRE leads.

Data collected / evidence snapshot (saved in ticket SRE‑4123):
- BGP syslog snippets (timestamps and withdrawn prefixes).
- tcpdump traces (pcap) from peering nodes and one affected customer edge (filtered to control plane IPs).
- Traceroutes from multiple locations (eu, us‑west, apac) showing divergence at customer border.
- Control plane logs showing TLS handshake timeouts and x509 validation errors timestamped to flap window.

Post‑incident action items (short list / owners):
- (Owner: Network) Add BGP prefix‑presence monitor: alert if any control plane prefix is withdrawn for > 60s from expected AS path. (SRE‑4130)
- (Owner: Product Security) Add guidance to Private deployment onboarding: require customer NOCs to whitelist control‑plane prefixes and avoid route‑map transforms during maintenance windows. (SRE‑4131)
- (Owner: Platform Eng) Evaluate advertising an optional /24 aggregate for control plane reachability as a fallback to reduce specificity risk; add config flag for customers who opt‑in. (SRE‑4132)
- (Owner: SRE) Update runbook with specific tcpdump/traceroute checks and sample commands (see runbook section below). (SRE‑4133)
- (Owner: Support) Draft customer‑facing postmortem note and guidance on firewall conntrack settings and asymmetric routing. (SRE‑4134)

Runbook sketch: Oncall steps when control plane reachability degraded for Private/VPC deployments

Purpose: Short procedures for first responders to quickly triage whether an outage is due to on‑prem routing/firewall changes vs. Redwood control plane fault. This is a sketch — feedback needed, convert to checked playbook.

Prechecks (first 5 minutes):
1) Confirm alert in Redwood Console and check scope (which tenants/regions) -> identify control plane IP(s).
2) Run traceroute from at least two Redwood vantage points:
   - traceroute -T -p <control_port> <control_ip>
   - Expected: hop path reaches customer edge and then to customer internal — if path stops at their border, likely on‑prem change.
3) Query BGP telemetry for withdrawals of the control prefix:
   - bgpctl show rib | grep <control_ip> (or equivalent; use fabric telemetry)
   - If we see WITHDRAW for prefix from customer AS within flap window -> route change likely.
4) If BGP withdraw observed, page Network team and contact customer NOC (use oncall contact sheet).

Quick network checks (commands and heuristics):
- From peering node / border router: show ip bgp <control_prefix> detail
  - look for: availability, AS path, community/localpref tags, last update time
- From affected customer edge (if we have VPN/ops access): tcpdump -i <iface> host <control_ip> and port <control_port>
  - look for TCP SYNs with no SYN‑ACK, or RSTs coming from router/firewall
- Check conntrack/nat table on customer firewall (requires customer cooperation): sudo conntrack -L | grep <control_ip>
- Check for route‑maps or policy changes in recent config commits on customer router (ask NOC for commit id).

Temporary mitigations (only escalate to these if customer rollback delayed > 10m):
- Reannounce aggregate towards customer AS (Network owner only): create a less specific route that avoids being filtered by route‑maps. Note: this is a temporary and opinionated step — coordinate with network lead and customer.
- If asymmetric routing observed with firewall RSTs: ask customer to disable stateful deep packet inspection for control plane prefixes during maintenance.

Runbook checklist — commands and expected indicators
- traceroute -T -p 443 <control_ip> -> shows where path stops (border hop vs deeper)
- bgpctl show adj‑ribs / show ip bgp <prefix> -> withdrawn? last update?
- tcpdump -i <iface> host <control_ip> and port <control_port> -> SYN only? RSTs?
- curl -v --connect‑timeout 3 https://<control_ip>:<port>/health -> TCP handshake or TLS failure details
- journalctl -u redwood‑agent -f on an affected host -> cert handshake timeouts and error class

Sample outputs we consider catastrophic vs transient:
- Catastrophic: immediate BGP withdrawal with no reannouncement for > 2m and tcpdump shows no SYN‑ACK or RSTs — indicates policy/blackhole.
- Transient: frequent reannouncements and tcpdump shows SYN/SYN‑ACK but heavy latency — likely convergence and not outright blackhole.

Runbook additions (permanent changes recommended):
- Add a preflight verification step to customer maintenance playbooks that checks BGP RIB for presence of control prefixes before committing route‑map changes.
- Add automated 'prefix presence' e2e test that runs from multiple Redwood vantage points and pings control IPs every 30s; if multiple vantage points report loss, trigger higher severity.
- Offer a recommended firewall rule template for customers:
  - Allow ingress/egress for control plane IPs on ports <control_port list> with no application inspection.
  - Use static NAT for control plane IPs to avoid conntrack asymmetry during route changes.

Customer communication / template language (for Support to adapt):
- "We observed that a recent route‑map change removed advertisement of control plane prefixes from your edge, causing temporary loss of reachability. For future maintenance windows please ensure the control plane prefixes listed in your onboarding doc remain advertised or coordinate with Redwood SRE on a maintenance plan. We've proposed a validation step you can add to your change script — see linked doc SRE‑4131."

Notes to self / unresolved questions:
- Do we want to require customers to accept an optional config flag that gives Redwood permission to advertise a less specific aggregate as a safety net? Legal/Procops needs to review.
- Can we get BGP update stream into an automated guardrail that blocks certain changes (e.g., withdraw of any prefix in the control plane list) or at least autorespond with a higher severity?
- Investigate whether our peering fabric could opportunistically set BGP community tags to protect control prefixes from customer route‑maps (needs deep network policy discussion).

Appendix A — quick forensic checklist for packet captures:
- Correlate SYN timestamps from customer edge with SYN timestamps on peering node; if SYN seen only on one side, asymmetry likely.
- Look for TTL differences and TCP window sizes that might indicate NAT or inspection.
- Search for ICMP unreachable messages that indicate NAT or ACL denies.

Appendix B — owners and deadlines (initial sprint):
- Network: SRE‑4130 (BGP presence monitor) — prototype by 2025‑11‑19.
- Platform Eng: SRE‑4132 (aggregate option) — proposal by 2025‑12‑03.
- Support: SRE‑4134 (customer comms) — draft by 2025‑11‑14.

This doc is a working sketch intended to capture early oncall notes and a runnable first version of a runbook. Additions welcome (especially concrete commands for our fabric telemetry systems and more examples of tcpdump shows).

Unstructured rough notes (fragments):
- Customer NOC used Junos 18.4, route‑map had match community 999:500 -> set next‑hop reject? double‑check commit.
- One tenant additionally had firewall with connection tracking timeout of 30s — explains why long‑lived sessions dropped.
- Consider adding a small synthetic probe from customer edge (via agent) that alerts customer NOC before Redwood triggers page.

End of notes.
